title: Sold Unopened
logline: On a low red cliff above a flat, shallow sea stand the brick stumps of a governor's house, built in 1802 to watch a pearl fishery out on the banks, on a bed of pearl-oyster shell the sea is now eating. What the fishery sold each evening was a closed shell, counted by the thousand, that nobody had seen inside: the record of that sale holds wanting with gladness and without, urged on and not, and the texts rank the calm kind the heavier.
human_question: If I can want something I have not seen, cannot taste and do not even enjoy, what exactly is the wanting fastened to, and why should the calm version of it weigh more than the excited one?

place.what_kind_of_place: A ruined colonial house on a wild, empty coast. A low cliff of red earth, four or five metres high, runs along a curved beach facing west over a shallow, usually flat sea; behind it is thorn scrub and sand with almost nothing standing above head height. On the cliff edge stand the remains of a two-storey house of about 1802 to 1804, designed by the governor of the day with a Greek Doric colonnade: what is left is a cluster of thick red-brick piers and wall stubs, one storey at most, with a tree grown up through the middle, and the footings of lost rooms running out to the cliff edge and stopping in air. A few hundred metres along the edge stands a tall stone obelisk. Under the turf of the cliff top lies a dense bed of small, flat pearl-oyster shells, the waste of centuries of pearl fishing, which shows in the cliff face where the sea cuts it. Nobody lives on the site; the fishery it was built for ended a century ago and the camps that served it have vanished.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. Red brick against a flat turquoise sea and a very large sky, with the ruin standing so close to the edge that sea shows through its piers from both sides. The cliff face itself, a cut section through soil and a pale band packed with shell, grains trickling down it in the wind, and the brick footings of rooms that end where the land ends. And the evening over open water to the west: this coast faces the sunset, the sea in the fishing season is often like a millpond, and the house was sited so that its roof commanded exactly that horizon.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Light and water only. The sun comes round from behind the ruin to set over the sea in front of it; the brick goes from dull brown to red to black. The small surf works at the foot of the cliff. Wind moves the scrub and dries grains of earth and shell off the exposed section. Nothing is built, sold, landed or carried on this shore now, and the film shows it that way: the whole apparatus of the fishery, boats, pens, auction and camp, exists only in the voice and in the shell.
place.when_it_looks_best: February to April, the old fishing season, when the north-east monsoon has eased and the sea is calmest, from late afternoon to last light. The film is one late afternoon into dusk: no dawn, no noon, no night.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The last-light film seen from below. It opens at sea level on the beach, looking up at the cliff: a line of red earth with brick stumps and a tree on the skyline, shot on a long lens from a tripod so that ruin, obelisk and sky stack flat. Then the cliff face at arm's length, soil above and a pale band of shell below, bits falling in the wind. Then the tops of lost walls running to the edge and ending in air. Then, once, the drone: not a reveal and not a move, but a single hover, held still at the height where the house's upper floor and roof terrace used to be, looking west over empty water while the sun goes down. The camera never pushes in, orbits or climbs past the ruin. Sound is wind and small surf only. It has its own shape without a word said: an odd building on an empty coast, what it is standing on, and the view it was built for with nothing in it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice supplies what the frame is missing: the fishery the house was built to watch, and the thing the fishery sold. In later years, each evening, the government's share of the day's catch was auctioned in lots of a thousand oysters, unopened; people bought single shells and handfuls in what an officer of the 1790s called oyster lotteries; the whole fishery was sometimes let to one renter for a fixed sum paid before an oyster came up. The texts of this group describe wanting as one thing set by three dials, with gladness or without it, with an excusing view or without, arising by itself or urged on, and they rank the flat kind above the glad one. The film lays the dials on documents, never on a person: a chaplain's book that sorts buyers by aim, a printed inspection notice that one writer calls an invitation to speculate and another a brake on it, a rental arrangement proposed as carrying no risk. The second concept follows the lot itself through the three tastes the texts allow, neither pleasant nor unpleasant as a closed shell, unpleasant as ten days of rot, pleasant as a pearl for the few, and ends on a telegram announcing that the oysters were all dead: pleasant feeling counted as a cause of pain by changing. The payoff hover is the governor's own sightline, the fishery's view, held on an empty sea.

sequence.on_screen: Late afternoon, from the wet sand at the foot of the cliff. Tripod, long lens, locked: a line of red earth, on its skyline a knot of brick piers with a tree through them, and further along the edge a stone obelisk. Small surf in the foreground. Held for a long time.
sequence.voice: In 1802 the British governor Frederick North laid the first stone of a house on this cliff, to his own design, with columns in the Greek Doric order. It was meant to be lived in a few weeks at a time, by a governor come to watch a fishery that happened out at sea, a few weeks in a good year and not at all in a bad one.

sequence.on_screen: The cliff face at arm's length, 50mm, still: turf on top, then earth, then a thick pale band packed with small flat shells, whole and broken. A few grains break loose and run down the face in the wind.
sequence.voice: What the house stands on is the fishery's waste. Archaeologists who dug beside the ruin found a bed of pearl-oyster shell under the soil, part of it dated to between the fifteenth and seventeenth centuries, long before the house. The sea takes some of it every year. Descriptions of the house say its walls were faced with lime burnt from the same shells.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level on the cliff top, looking west past the brick stubs to the horizon. Flat sea, nothing on it. Locked.
sequence.voice: What this fishery sold was a closed shell. From the start people bought single oysters and handfuls, unopened, in what an army officer of the 1790s, Robert Percival, called oyster lotteries. In 1804 the whole fishery was let to one renter for a fixed sum before a single shell came up. In its later years the government's share of each day's catch was counted by the thousand and auctioned at sunset, still closed.

sequence.on_screen: The footings of lost rooms: low courses of brick running across the turf to the cliff edge and ending in air, the sea below. Wind in the scrub. Locked, wide.
sequence.voice: The texts describe wanting that comes with gladness and wanting that comes with none, on an object neither pleasing nor displeasing, and they rank the flat kind heavier. A closed shell bought at a posted price is about as close to such an object as a market can offer. Calm, in these texts, is not the same as innocent.

sequence.on_screen: The obelisk against the evening sky, long lens from the beach, the brick of the ruin soft in the foreground. Locked.
sequence.voice: The government printed the result of each inspection of the banks before a fishery. The chaplain James Cordiner, who stayed in this house in 1804, says it was printed so that people meaning to speculate could judge their chances. A visitor a century later says it was meant to keep the speculation within bounds. One notice, read as a spur and as a brake. The texts count wanting urged on by someone else as its own kind, and the lesser one, but they do not excuse it.

sequence.on_screen: Dusk coming on. The ruin from the landward side, piers black against the last colour, sea showing between them. Locked. The wind is the only sound.
sequence.voice: The same chaplain sorted the buyers of closed shells into two columns: speculators for profit, and a few merely for amusement. It is a sentence about other people's aims, written by a man who could no more see them than this camera can. The texts sort wanting the same way, with gladness or without, with an excuse or without, by itself or urged on. A column in a book is not a reading of anyone's mind, and this film does not offer one.

sequence.on_screen: The cliff face again, now nearly in shadow, the band of shell just readable. Then the beach below, grey, the surf small.
sequence.voice: Whatever was bought here went through three tastes, in order. First a closed shell, neither pleasant nor unpleasant. Then about ten days of rot in the pens on the shore, a smell Cordiner called the most nauseous that can be experienced, though he adds that the men who worked beside it stopped noticing it. Then, for some, a pearl. The texts say every moment tastes its object in one of those three ways, and that there is no fourth.

sequence.on_screen: The single drone shot. A hover, held perfectly still at the height where the house's upper floor and roof terrace stood, looking due west over empty water as the sun reaches the horizon and goes. No move, no turn, no descent. Cut to black on the last light.
sequence.voice: From the roof, Cordiner wrote, there was a fine view of the line of boats coming back from the banks. In 1864 a telegram went round the fishing coasts: there will be no pearl fishery this year, oysters all dead. The texts say that pleasant feeling, not painful by its nature, becomes a cause of pain by changing. They mean it as a count, not as a mood. This is the view the house was built for.

concept_merge.why_together: C006 carries the film because the fishery's own record sorts wanting along the same three dials the sources use, and puts the result on paper rather than on a face. The Margaya gives eight greed-rooted minds by gladness or its absence, by the presence of a view that excuses the act, and by whether the mind arises of itself or is urged on by another or by one's own coaxing [C006-M:L5]; it ranks view-backed above view-free, unprompted above prompted, and neutral above joyful [C006-M:L19]. The Pradeepika ties neutral feeling to a neutral object, one neither pleasing nor displeasing [C006-P:L74]. A lot of a thousand unopened oysters sold at a posted price is as close to such an object as any market has offered; eyewitnesses in 1797 and 1804 wrote down buyers' aims as profit and amusement; the printed inspection notice is read by one writer as an invitation to speculate and by another as a brake. C032 follows the object instead of the buyer. Feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, present in every mind and varying with the object [C032-P:L43], and it has three modes with no fourth [C032-M:L5]: the fishery's lot passes through all three in ten days, and the fishery itself ends in the Pradeepika's suffering of change, pleasant feeling that becomes a cause of pain by changing [C032-P:L117].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That wanting does not need a pleasant object in front of it, and that the texts do not treat its calm, uninterested form as the lighter one. C006 alone would make this a film about a gamble, and a gamble invites the easy picture of excited people, which the film may not show and the texts do not favour: they rank the flat kind heavier. C032 alone would make it a film about a smell and a jewel. Together they separate the wanting from the tasting: the buying happened on a closed shell whose flavour was not yet anything at all, the tasting came later and went through all three tones, and the whole trade ended in the change the Pradeepika counts as pain. The ruin is the one object on the shore that watched all of it and is now itself changing, into the sea.

concept_links.why: The Margaya sorts the eight greed-rooted minds by joy or its absence, by a view that excuses the act, and by prompting, which it defines to include being urged on by another and coaxing one's own hesitating mind [C006-M:L5] [C006-M:L9]; its examples of view are self-serving excuses, 'no fault in taking what the rich have spare', 'no fault in taking ill-gotten wealth', 'the gods gave us these' [C006-M:L3] [C006-M:L11]. It then ranks view-backed above view-free, unprompted above prompted, and neutral above joyful [C006-M:L19]. The Pradeepika explains neutral feeling as arising on a neutral object, neither pleasing nor displeasing [C006-P:L74], and joyful feeling as arising on meeting a pleasing one [C006-P:L25]. The fishery's record asks this question in its own categories, not by analogy: it sold, by the thousand and unopened, an object nobody could yet find pleasing; an officer who attended the fisheries of the 1790s called the small purchases oyster lotteries; the chaplain who stayed in the house in 1804 wrote that buyers bought 'with a view of profit, and by a few merely for amusement'; the published inspection was described in 1807 as issued so that speculators could 'judge of the probability of success' and in 1912 as meant to keep 'the speculative fever within reasonable limits'. The film lays every dial on a document or a rule, never on a person, and says in its own voice that a column in a book is not a reading of a mind. does_not_transfer lines that bind it: 'Calm means good' is exactly what the film contradicts, on the Margaya's own ranking, and the voice says calm is not innocence; 'I was pressured, so it's not on me' is contradicted in the notice beat, where the voice says the texts count urged-on wanting as the lesser kind but do not excuse it; ''Wrong view' must not be mapped onto any community's faith' rules out every religious element of the historical fishery (charm-binders, shares paid to temples), none of which appears; and no buyer, diver, renter or merchant is shown or described as wanting. The film does not assign any documented view to any person or body: the dispute over whether fishing exhausted the banks is kept in the research, not in the voice, because no source shows anyone holding the view that it had no consequence.

The Pradeepika defines feeling as the tasting of an object's flavour, present in every mind because every mind takes an object, and varying with the kind of object [C032-P:L43]; the Margaya says the flavour is tasted as sweet, as unsweet, or as neutral, and that there is no fourth way [C032-M:L5]. The fishery's lot passes through all three tones in order, as documented by the eyewitness who stayed in the house: a closed shell, about ten days of putrefaction in the pens with a stench 'the most nauseous that can ever be experienced', then the pearls. The Pradeepika's suffering of change, pleasant feelings that are not painful by nature but become a cause of pain by changing [C032-P:L117], is the fishery's own ending, recorded in an 1864 telegram announcing no fishery because the oysters were all dead; the related suffering of the conditioned, rise and fall [C032-P:L115], is on screen in the cliff. The film deliberately does not use the group's 'bodily pleasure has one seat, touch' argument, which another GRP-02 proposal builds on. does_not_transfer lines that bind it: 'Life is suffering' as pessimism is ruled out, and the voice says the texts mean change as a count, not a mood; 'Pleasure is the enemy' is ruled out, and nothing in the film disparages the pearl or its beauty; 'Neutral means numb' is respected by never calling the closed shell's neutrality an absence of mind; 'Chase good vibes' does not arise. The digest flags that the Pradeepika's own wording of neutral feeling [C032-P:L75] reads as if the object were moderately pleasing, unlike C006-P:L74; the film therefore calls the closed shell 'neither pleasant nor unpleasant' only in the Margaya's terms and does not lean on the disputed line.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That in these texts wanting is one thing with three settings, gladness or none, an excuse or none, self-started or urged on, and that the flat, calm, reasoned setting is ranked the heavier; that wanting can fasten on something that has not yet been tasted at all, and that the tasting, when it comes, is always one of three tones and never a fourth; that a record of other people's aims, like a chaplain's two columns, is not a reading of their minds; and that even a pleasant thing is counted as pain in the sense that it changes. All of it is carried by footage that asks no belief: a building made for watching, the shell it stands on, and the empty sea it watched.
what_must_be_real: The ruin, the cliff, the shell band and the sea exactly as they are on the day, in natural light. No reconstruction of the fishery: no boats dressed as pearling boats, no oysters bought or rotted for the camera, no actors, no archive-style re-enactment. The shell in the cliff is filmed where it is and never dug, picked or disturbed; the site is a protected monument and the midden is an archaeological deposit. No present-day fishing, landing or trading on this coast is filmed at all, and nobody who lives nearby is filmed as part of the story. The quotations in the voice are from the printed sources as read; the 1864 telegram is quoted as reported by a historian from the archive and is labelled as such in the research.
position_hint: Mid-group, after the films that set out the three dials of wanting on land (the weather film and the throne film) and before the films about desire-to-act: this one puts the heaviest of the dials, the calm one, on an object nobody could see, and hands C032's three tones to the group's later feeling films. It is the group's only ruin and its only film on the sea's edge at sunset.
risks: Turning the pearl trade into a morality tale about colonial greed. The charge sits on documents and rules (the auction of closed lots, the rental of the fishery, the printed notice), never on North, Cordiner, any renter, diver or merchant, and never on the colonial government as a mind.

Framing divers or buyers as wanting. Sources used for research describe divers concealing pearls and declaring banks exhausted when tired, and describe crowds of 'gamblers, vagrants, and rogues'; none of this enters the film. Livelihoods are not destinies: the divers' third of the catch is mentioned only as wages, if at all.

Mapping 'wrong view' onto faith. The historical fishery had religious elements (charm-binders paid in oysters, shares for temples on the opposite coast); none appears. The chaplain's sentences about which communities were most active in trade, and the 1912 visitor's racial typologies, never enter the voice in any form.

Civil war. The coast was a conflict zone and the wider division has been demined; the film's history is 1797 to 1925 plus the archaeology, and nothing of the war is shown or said. Present-day land and resettlement disputes in the division are not entered; the later fishery camp site further south, which lies inside that dispute, is not filmed or named.
Bereavement register. The fishery's cholera outbreaks and the 1907 financial panic, in which merchants died, are not used. 'Oysters all dead' is about oysters and is read flatly.
The ruin as romance. The voice never calls the ruin melancholy or the empty sea mournful; C032's suffering of change is stated as a count, per its does_not_transfer.

Over-claiming the neutral object. The texts do not say a closed shell is a neutral object; the voice says only that the texts rank wanting on a neither-pleasing-nor-displeasing object heavier, and describes the shell. Whether any buyer's feeling was neutral is unknowable and is never said.
Duplicating the whale-watching proposal's argument (sight gives no bodily pleasure). Avoided by design: this film's C032 strand is the three tones and change.

Adjudicating the ruin's folk identification. Local tradition has attached the ruin to a legendary queen; the research records that the builder is documented, but the film does not mention the tradition at all rather than correct a living belief.
Fort archetype. A small Dutch fort ruin lies about 1.3 km north; it is not filmed, so the film does not repeat the slate's fort.
drop_if: The ruin has lost further standing fabric since the last published photographs (2018 to 2019) so that little stands above the turf.

Drone flight on this coast is refused and no ground position gives the western sightline from about the height of the lost upper floor (a mast, a ladder platform or the obelisk base are the only alternatives).
The Department of Archaeology or the local authorities do not allow filming of the cliff section, or the band of shell is not visible in the face at the time of shooting.
The site or its approach turns out not to be cleared of mines, or is inside a restricted military or naval zone.
The chunam-of-oyster-shell claim cannot be sourced to a document before the shoot; the voice line then drops that sentence rather than the film.

connections.note: The group's weather film puts C006's conditions for the sharp, unprompted mind (health, climate, food) on a colonial plain built as a place to be well, and holds a frost melting at dawn in macro. This film takes the other end of the same text, the flat, neutral, reasoned kind that the Margaya ranks heavier, and puts it on an object nobody could see. Dawn, cold, close and still there; last light, heat, wide and still here, with one hover and no macro.

Another group's film on the same flat salt coast of the north-west: a thorn tree brought in on purpose that now has to be dug out root by root. Both are about something done to this coast for a reason; that film's work is still going on and is filmed, this one's ended a century ago and exists only in shell and brick. Birds, mud and saws there; one ruin, one cliff and an empty sea here.

Another group's film on a colonial fort whose walls are packed with burnt coral and reused stone, opened up in cross-section. This film also reads a colonial building's substance, here lime reportedly burnt from the shells it stands on, but it is a house built to watch a trade, not a fortification, and it keeps the nearby small fort out of frame so the fort archetype is not repeated.

Proposed in the GRP-02 selection (still being written): an open-sea film on a whale-watching ground and a shipping lane, carrying C032 through sight that gives no bodily pleasure and through suffering concealed at sea. Both are GRP-02 sea films about a pleasure sold; that one is water-borne, pre-dawn and moving with an animal, this one never leaves the shore, is shot at last light, and carries C032 through the three tones and the suffering of change instead.

selection.reason: Kept on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal after testing it, with its facts corrected and its treatment replaced. The proposal's story holds: an eyewitness chaplain's 1807 account (the 1804 fishery, written from this house) and an officer's 1803 account (the fisheries of the 1790s) document the sale of unopened oysters, the 'oyster lotteries', the rental of the whole fishery and the published inspection, and a 2024 excavation documents the pearl-oyster midden the ruin stands on. Corrected: the 1905 police quotation about gamblers belongs to a later camp further south and is not used; 'a beach of oyster shell' is wrong, the shell is under soil and shows in the eroding cliff; the widely repeated completion date of 11 February 1804 is the chaplain's date for the governor's arrival; the house was already a ruin when photographed in February 1902. The proposal's golden-hour drone over middens was replaced by a tripod film from below and a single static hover. Weaknesses stated: the C006 fit is a sale whose categories match the text's, not a story that argues about wanting; the surviving ruin is small; drone and access are unverified.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C006 primary, C032 supporting). The title changed from 'Upstream of the Rice' (kept in aliases) to 'Sold Unopened'. The location, proposed by Claude, is the ruin of Governor Frederick North's house of 1802 to 1804 on a low cliff of the north-west coast, and the pearl-oyster midden it stands on; it was the blind selection's proposal, tested and kept with several facts corrected. The film lays C006's three dials on the fishery's documents, not on any person: the auction of the government's share in unopened lots of a thousand, the 'oyster lotteries' named by Robert Percival (1803), James Cordiner's 1807 sorting of buyers into those buying for profit and a few for amusement, and the printed inspection that Cordiner reads as an invitation to speculate and a 1912 writer as a brake. It uses the Margaya's ranking of neutral over joyful wanting and says in the voice that calm is not innocence. C032 follows the lot through the three tones (closed shell, rot, pearl) and ends on the suffering of change in an 1864 telegram, 'oysters all dead'. Treatment: February to April, late afternoon to last light, tripod and long lens from the beach below the cliff, one arm's-length frame of the shell band, and a single drone shot, a static hover at the height of the lost upper floor looking west at an empty sea as the sun sets; no reveal, no orbit, no macro, no music. Its district moves from 4 to 5 films (see suggested_location.research_note). Unverified: current state of the ruin after 2004, drone and naval clearance, mine clearance of the approach, the documentary source for the oyster-shell lime, and the telegram's archival text, which was reached only through a historian's article.

suggested_location.region: Mannar District, Northern Province: the Musali division on the mainland coast south of Mannar Island, on the low cliffed shore of the bight between Arippu and Silavathurai, facing west over the Gulf of Mannar; Arippu village and its small Dutch fort ruin are about 1.3 km to the north
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one surviving building of the pearl fishery that ran off this coast for centuries, and it was built for the purpose the film needs: to watch. The governor's chaplain, who stayed in it in 1804, says its roof terrace gave a view of the open sea and of the line of boats returning from the banks. It stands on the fishery's own waste, a dense pearl-oyster midden that archaeologists excavated beside it and dated in part before the European period, and which the sea is now cutting into. The documents that carry C006, the sale of closed lots, the oyster lotteries, the rental of the fishery, the printed inspection, describe the fishery this house was built to oversee. And the frame is real: red brick on a red cliff over a flat western sea, empty of people, at sunset.

historical_thread.story: Pearl oysters (Pinctada fucata) were fished from banks ten to twenty miles off this coast for centuries before the British. Herdman's report of 1903 notes that at the time Ribeyro wrote (1685) Arippu was already the centre of the northern fisheries. The last Dutch fishery was in 1768 and the first under British control in 1796. Robert Percival, an army officer who attended the fisheries of the late 1790s, published in 1803 that 'oyster lotteries are carried on here to a great extent; they consist of purchasing a quantity of the oysters unopened, and running the chance of either finding or not finding pearls in them', adding that 'the European officers and gentlemen, who attend here upon duty or through curiosity' very frequently made such purchases. Governor Frederick North laid the first stone of a two-storey house on the cliff on 18 March 1802, to his own Doric design; it was finished by early 1804. James Cordiner, late chaplain to the garrison at Colombo, stayed there during the 1804 fishery and published in 1807 an account with an engraved plate of the house: 'undoubtedly the most beautiful building in the island', two miles north of the scene of the fishery, with a roof terrace giving 'a fine view of the line of boats, when they are returning from the banks'. North arrived there on 11 February 1804. Cordiner records that the result of each inspection of the banks 'is published in such a manner as to enable persons intending to speculate in the concern to judge of the probability of success'; that the 1804 fishery was let to a single renter, who undertook to pay 300,000 Porto Novo pagodas (£120,000) for thirty days' fishing with 150 boats, and that 'the general expectation was greatly disappointed'; that the renter's oysters were piled in heaps and not opened until the fishery was well advanced; that the divers' oysters were bought 'in small quantities by a variety of speculators, with a view of profit, and by a few merely for amusement', and that 'there is scarcely a gentleman or servant of any description present at the scene, who does not every day lay out a small sum in an adventure of this nature'; that oysters were left about ten days 'to render them putrid' and then washed in canoes, where 'the stench... is the most nauseous that can ever be experienced; and a person who is led there merely by curiosity, does not remain long near it. The labourers and overseers, however, from habit become insensible of the smell'. He also gives the rentals: the 1797 fishery bought for upwards of £110,000, 1798 for £140,400, the average daily landing per boat falling from twelve thousand to eight thousand to six thousand, and in 1799 'the banks having been exhausted by the three preceding fisheries, it only yielded 30,000l.' He recommends renting boats individually to 'a multitude of adventurers', two-thirds paid in advance, so that 'there could be no risque of sustaining any loss'. Through the nineteenth century the fishery's defining feature, in Herdman's words, was 'their uncertainty and intermittent character': by the list compiled by Hornell there were only 36 fisheries in the century, with failures from 1820 to 1828, 1837 to 1854 and 1864 to 1873. The historian Tamara Fernando quotes from the archive a telegram of 1864: 'Please circulate information that there will be no Pearl Fishery at Arippo Ceylon this year: Oysters all dead.' The camp moved south to Silavathurai in the 1850s and to Marichchukaddi from 1889. The Ceylon government engaged W. A. Herdman, who reached the island in January 1902; in February 1902 he photographed the Doric, 'built by Lord Guildford a century ago... but being unused it later on fell into ruins', and an old cannon near it nearly toppled by the erosion of the coast. His report names two dangers, overcrowding and overfishing, and says there is 'no reason for any despondency in regard to the future of the pearl fisheries, if they are treated scientifically'. In 1906 the banks were leased to the Ceylon Company of Pearl Fishers at £20,666 a year; Churchill told the Commons that Herdman 'did not consider that the company could make their bargain a paying concern'. By Hugh M. Smith's account of 1912, the government's share was counted by clerks and auctioned about sunset in lots of a thousand; its advance estimate of pearl value per thousand had 'the praiseworthy object, if it does not have the effect, of keeping the speculative fever within reasonable limits'; and since the lease there had been 'no fishery worth mentioning'. The company failed in 1912; the colonial series of fisheries ends in 1925. The house was declared a protected monument by gazette on 16 August 2013. A 2024 excavation beside it found a compact pearl-oyster midden on the cliff at about 4.3 m above sea level, one shell dated 1424-1673 cal CE, the Arippu middens covering about 0.4 km² and 'more extensive before the sea eroded them away', and reported that the bungalow was built with lime made from pearl-oyster shells.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C006's question is not whether people wanted pearls but what kind of wanting it was: with gladness or without, with an excusing view or without, of itself or urged on, and which of these weighs most. The fishery's record already asks it in its own categories. It sold, every evening, a closed object that could not yet be pleasing or displeasing; the Pradeepika ties neutral feeling to exactly such an object [C006-P:L74] and the Margaya ranks neutral-feeling wanting above the joyful kind [C006-M:L19]. The eyewitnesses sort buyers' aims into profit and amusement and name the small purchases lotteries; the film does not believe or disbelieve them, it says their sorting is a document, not a mind. The printed inspection is described a century apart as a spur and as a brake, which is the Margaya's prompting by another [C006-M:L5] with its direction undecided. And a chaplain proposes, in print, a rental arrangement in which the government 'could' run 'no risque of sustaining any loss': a calm, reasoned taking written as a rule, which the film shows the texts refuse to count as light. For C032 the same record follows the object: every mind tastes its object [C032-P:L43] in one of three ways with no fourth [C032-M:L5], and the lot went closed, rotten, then pearl; the trade ended in change counted as pain [C032-P:L117], documented as a telegram. The ruin binds both because it was built as the fishery's observation post and is made, by report, of the fishery's shell.
what_is_certain: Governor Frederick North laid the first stone of the house on 18 March 1802 (Wikipedia, Lanka Pradeepa, AmazingLanka, all citing Wisumperuma); it was built to oversee the pearl fishery.

James Cordiner's A Description of Ceylon (1807), vol. II, ch. XVI, describes the house from a stay during the 1804 fishery: design 'purely Doric... given by the Honourable Frederic North himself', two miles north of the scene of the fishery, a roof terrace with 'a fine view of the line of boats, when they are returning from the banks', and an engraved plate titled 'Governor's House at Aripo'. Read in the archive.org scan.
Cordiner states that North arrived at the government house at Aripo on 11 February (1804).
Percival (1803) names 'oyster lotteries', the purchase of oysters unopened, and says European officers and gentlemen very frequently made such purchases. Read in the archive.org scan.

Cordiner (1807) says small purchasers bought 'with a view of profit, and by a few merely for amusement'; that inspection results were published 'to enable persons intending to speculate... to judge of the probability of success'; that the 1804 fishery was let to one renter for 300,000 Porto Novo pagodas (£120,000) for thirty days with 150 boats; and that in 1799 the banks had been 'exhausted by the three preceding fisheries'. Read in the scan.

Cordiner describes about ten days' putrefaction and the washing canoes, with the full sentence on the stench and on labourers who 'from habit become insensible of the smell'. The film quotes both halves or neither.

Herdman photographed the house in ruins in February 1902 and wrote that, being unused, it 'later on fell into ruins' (Report, Part I, 1903, pp. 56-57, figs. 8-9); the ruin was already a ruin a century before the modern collapses.
Herdman's list gives only 36 fisheries in the nineteenth century, with the long failures 1820-28, 1837-54 and 1864-73.
The banks were leased in 1906 to the Ceylon Company of Pearl Fishers at £20,666 a year (Hansard, 25 June 1906).
Smith (1912) describes the government's share counted by clerks, auctioned about sunset in lots of a thousand, and the divers' retention of one third as wages.

Siriwardana, Dissanayake and Çakırlar (2024) excavated a pearl-oyster midden beside the ruin, on the cliff at about 430 cm above sea level, with an AMS date of 1424-1673 cal CE on a Pinctada fucata shell; they describe the Arippu middens as about 0.4 km² and eroding into the sea.
The house was declared a protected archaeological monument by gazette notification of 16 August 2013 (Lanka Pradeepa).

District: the OpenStreetMap node for the ruin (8.7809, 79.9344) reverse-geocodes to Mannar District, Northern Province, and falls inside the Mannar District boundary polygon; the Musali division is from published descriptions.
what_is_disputed: Completion date. Wikipedia gives construction as 18 March 1802 to 11 February 1804; 11 February is the date Cordiner gives for North's arrival at the house, not for its completion. Other sources say 'early 1804' or 'almost two years'. Both are recorded; neither is averaged.

The collapses. Wikipedia and AmazingLanka: the rear (seaward, western) portico lost in the 1980s or 'after 1980', and the northern section collapsed in 2004; Lanka Pradeepa: northern wall sections collapsed 'in or after 2003'. The state of the ruin since the last dated photographs (2018, 2019) is not known.

Identification. The ruin has been attached by tradition to a legendary queen (Alli Rani) and confused with the Dutch fort and with a Portuguese building; Wisumperuma's paper addresses this but was not reached (HTTP 403). The film does not mention the tradition.

The oyster-shell lime. That the facing (chunam) was burnt from pearl-oyster shell is stated by Wikipedia, AmazingLanka and the 2024 excavation report; the documentary source it rests on (North's correspondence or Public Works records) was not reached. It appears in the voice only as 'descriptions of the house say'.

The notice's purpose. Cordiner (1807) reads the published inspection as a guide for speculators; Smith (1912) as meant to keep 'the speculative fever within reasonable limits', 'if it does not have the effect'. The film holds both readings.

Whether fishing exhausted the banks. Cordiner (1807) says the 1799 fishery failed because the banks were 'exhausted by the three preceding fisheries'; Herdman (1903) lists overfishing among the causes but judges it 'comparatively rarely' serious beside natural mortality, sand and predators, and Smith (1912) puts the destruction 'principally' on physical agencies and enemies. The 2024 archaeologists read shell size as a measure of exploitation pressure and find the Arippu sample smaller than the all-site mean, without, in the passages read, drawing a firm conclusion for this site. The film keeps this dispute out of the voice.

Where the 1804 fishery happened. Cordiner puts the scene at Kondachchi, two to three miles south of the house; Fernando says fisheries were 'held from Arippo' 1796-1837. These are the same bight named from different points, but the auction and the pens were not at the house itself; the voice says 'this coast', never 'this spot'.

The police chief's 1905 remark about 'gamblers, vagrants, and rogues' quoted by Smith (1912) concerns the camp at Marichchukaddi, about ten miles south, and is secondhand; the blind proposal attached it to this site. It is not used.

what_to_film: From the wet sand at the foot of the cliff, on a tripod, 85-135mm: the cliff line with the brick piers and the tree on the skyline, the obelisk further along, sky and small surf. Late afternoon to dusk.
The cliff section at arm's length, 50mm, locked: turf, soil and the pale band of pearl-oyster shell, with grains falling in the wind. Not macro, not touched.
The footings of lost rooms running to the cliff edge and ending in air, wide, from the landward side.
The ruin from the landward side at dusk, piers black against the last colour, sea visible between them.
The obelisk against the evening sky, compressed with the ruin.

The single drone shot: a hover held still at the approximate height of the lost upper floor and roof terrace (height not documented; to be estimated from Cordiner's plate), facing due west, from the sun a few degrees above the horizon until after it sets. No move.
Not filmed: the Dutch fort ruin, present-day fishing boats or landings, the villages, the later camp sites to the south, any person as a subject.
suggested_location.access: By road on the coast route south of Mannar through the Musali division; travel blogs (2017) describe entry to the ruin as unrestricted, with no guard or ticket, and a walk on the beach below. The monument is gazetted, so a Department of Archaeology permit is needed for professional filming. Drone flight needs Civil Aviation Authority clearance and, on this northern coast, Ministry of Defence and possibly Navy clearance; unverified. The division was mined during the war and has been under clearance; the approach and the beach below the cliff must be confirmed as cleared before any crew leaves the track. The cliff edge is unstable and the ruin is not safe to climb or enter.
suggested_location.best_time: February to April, the historical fishing season, for a calm sea and clear western horizon; from about two hours before sunset to last light. The south-west monsoon (roughly May to September) brings strong wind and rough water on this coast and would change the film.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 2026-09-26. Primary texts read directly in archive.org scans: Percival (1803), Cordiner (1807, vol. II ch. XVI), Herdman (1903, Part I). Smith (1912) read in the lakdiva OCR text; Hansard 1906 read online; the 2024 excavation read in the open-access Springer text; Fernando (2022) read only through a reproduction and search summaries, so the 1864 telegram is secondhand (Fernando citing the Sri Lanka National Archives). Not reached: Wisumperuma's paper on the date and identification (academia.edu 403), the Daily Mirror feature (bot wall), Steuart's 1843 book (his 1833 paper was read and has nothing on the sales), Tennent's chapter (Tennent is named in another GRP-02 film and is deliberately not used here). District verified by reverse geocoding the OpenStreetMap node of the ruin (8.7809, 79.9344), which lies inside the Mannar District boundary; the blind proposal's 8.779, 79.930 is about 450 m off and was corrected. Mannar District moves from 4 to 5 films; no other GRP-02 or GRP-03 film is in Mannar. The other Mannar films are a wind farm on the island, pre-dawn kitchens, the Prosopis flats of the sanctuary and a demining film in the same division about 6 km inland; none is a ruin or a pearl film. Images: three Commons files confirmed through the API and viewed; the file named 'Doric Bungalow.jpg' shows the obelisk, not the house, and is captioned so. No image of the shell band in the cliff face was found. Nothing about access, permissions, drone clearance, mine clearance or the ruin's current state has been verified on the ground.

Whether the shell band is visible in the cliff face at the chosen stretch and season, and whether filming it is permitted.
The height of the lost upper floor and roof terrace, for the hover; to be estimated from Cordiner's plate and the surviving piers.
The primary source for the oyster-shell lime facing; Wisumperuma's paper was not reached.
The archival text of the 1864 telegram, reached only through Fernando (2022).
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. Percival (1803), Cordiner (1807) and Herdman (1903) are documentary and were read in scans of the printed texts; Smith (1912) and Hansard (1906) are documentary and were read online; the 2024 excavation is peer-reviewed archaeology read in full text; the 1864 telegram is documentary but reached only through a historian's article; the construction and collapse dates rest on secondary sources citing Wisumperuma, whose paper was not reached; access, permissions and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
